RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: A clay tablet from Ugarit, scratched about 1400 BCE, lists thirty signs in a fixed order and nothing else. The order is not the order of anything in the world, and it is not alphabetical in any sense the signs themselves could supply. It is nonetheless the order our own alphabet still runs _____ list of signs was already being recited and learned by heart as a sequence.
RW_M1.why: Two complete statements meet at the blank with no conjunction, so the first has to be closed before the second begins. The comma splices them, running one straight into the other.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: A wader that has just crossed an ocean cannot be followed to its feeding grounds, but it can be weighed. The team works the high-tide roost with mist nets, takes each bird's mass to the gram and lets it go within the hour, and the same flock is caught again eleven days later. Caught at the roost and weighed before release, _____
RW_M1.why: The opening phrase describes whatever was caught and weighed, and only birds can be, so the birds must be the subject of the clause that follows. Each of the other versions puts a period of time or a gain in that position, neither of which can be trapped at a roost.

choices.label: A
choices.content: it was found that a third of their arrival mass had been gained in eleven days.

choices.label: B
choices.content: a gain of a third of their arrival mass had taken eleven days.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the birds had gained a third of their arrival mass in eleven days.

choices.label: D
choices.content: eleven days had been enough for a gain of a third of their arrival mass.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: The mill at the bridge had ground on two pairs of stones since 1780, and it had taken the corn of six parishes. By the time the roller plant opened in the valley in 1889, the trade in stone-ground flour _____ already begun to fall away.
RW_M1.why: The falling away happens before the roller plant opens, and both events lie in the past, so the earlier one takes the past perfect. The present perfect would place the decline in a period reaching up to now, which the dates rule out.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M1.passage: The charcoal burner sleeps beside the stack for the whole of the burn, and a stack left unwatched for two hours can be lost. Each of the vents cut around the base of the clamp _____ opened and stopped again by hand as the smoke changes colour.
RW_M1.why: The subject is 'each', which is singular, and the words naming the vents sit inside a phrase that cannot change the number of the subject. The plural forms agree with 'vents' instead, which is not what the sentence is about.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M1.passage: The sacbeob are raised limestone roads, plastered white and in places ten metres across, and some run twenty miles from one centre to another. They were built in a country that had no wheeled vehicles and no pack animals, so everything moving along them moved on somebody's back. _____ they were made wide, level and hard enough to carry traffic of a kind that did not exist.
RW_M1.why: The width and hard surface stand against the absence of carts and animals that the sentence before has just established, so the transition marks that tension. A consequence relation would have the absence of vehicles producing the wide road, which reverses the sense.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M1.passage: Peat lifted from the bank is two-thirds water by weight, and a wet turf will not take a flame at all. The cutter stacks the turves in open lattices with the wind blowing through them, turns the stack twice before autumn and carts it home only when it rings under the hand. _____ a fuel that costs nothing to buy costs a summer of work before it will burn.
RW_M1.why: The summer of stacking and turning described in the second sentence is what produces the cost in labour stated in the third, so the transition marks a consequence. A contrast would require the last sentence to cut against the drying work, and it follows from it instead.

RW_M1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M1.passage: Soil organisms respond both to temperature and to how much water fills the pores between the grains, and neither factor on its own predicts what a soil will do. _____ a warm soil that is saturated gives off less carbon dioxide than a cool one that is merely damp, because the organisms in the wet soil are short of oxygen.
RW_M1.why: The second sentence supplies a particular case illustrating the general claim that one factor alone predicts nothing. A contrast would set the case against the claim, but the case is an instance of it.

RW_M1.stem: The student wants to explain how a single standard was made to reach an individual trader's measure. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Local measures varied from town to town across the kingdom.
  • From 1497 bronze standards were sent out to the market towns from the Exchequer.
  • Market officers compared the traders' measures against the town's bronze standard.
  • A measure that matched was stamped, and an unstamped measure could be seized.
  • The bronze standards were themselves copied from a single set kept in London.
RW_M1.why: The goal asks how the chain ran from the one original down to a trader's vessel, and only the choice following the copies out to the towns and then to the stamping of individual measures traces it. Stating that the standards were copied from a London set covers only the first link.

choices.label: A
choices.content: From 1497 bronze standards were sent out to the market towns.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Local measures varied from town to town across the kingdom.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The bronze standards were copied from a single set kept in London.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Copies of one London set were sent to the market towns, where officers compared each trader's measure against them and stamped the ones that matched.

RW_M1.stem: The student wants to explain why lime mortar is described as returning to the rock it came from. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Limestone is burned in a kiln, which drives carbon dioxide out of it and leaves quicklime.
  • Water added to quicklime slakes it into a putty.
  • Mortar made from the putty sets by taking carbon dioxide back out of the air.
  • The set material is calcium carbonate, the substance the limestone was made of.
  • A lime mortar goes on hardening for years as the change works inward from the surface.
RW_M1.why: The goal asks for the sense in which the material comes full circle, and only the choice pairing the carbon dioxide driven off in the kiln with the same gas taken back during the set completes the circle. The note about years of hardening describes the rate of the change rather than what the change produces.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Limestone is burned in a kiln, which drives carbon dioxide out of it.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Burning drives carbon dioxide out of the limestone and the set takes it back from the air, leaving the mortar as the same carbonate the stone was.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A lime mortar goes on hardening for years after it is laid.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Water added to quicklime slakes it into a putty.

RW_M1.stem: The student wants to explain why Maya dates can be placed more precisely than those of neighbouring cultures. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Maya monuments carry dates counted in days from a fixed starting point in 3114 BCE.
  • The count runs continuously and does not restart with a new ruler.
  • Neighbouring cultures dated events by the reign in which they fell.
  • A Long Count date can be placed to the individual day.
  • Fixing the whole count against the European calendar took scholars several decades.
RW_M1.why: The goal asks for a comparison, and only the choice setting a continuous count in days against dating by reign explains the difference in precision. The decades spent on the correlation concern modern scholarship rather than the precision of the original dates.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Fixing the count against the European calendar took scholars several decades.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Maya monuments carry dates counted in days from a fixed starting point.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Because the Maya count runs in days from one fixed point and does not restart with each ruler, a date can be placed to the day, while neighbouring cultures dated events by reign.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Neighbouring cultures dated events by the reign in which they fell.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2E.passage: A cob wall is raised from a stiff mixture of subsoil, straw and water thrown up in courses about half a metre high. Each course must dry and take its own weight before the next can go on, and the sides are pared back with a spade once they are firm. A wall of any height therefore takes a season and cannot be hurried, so building in cob is necessarily _____.
RW_M2E.why: The passage describes a wall that goes up one drying course at a time and cannot be pushed faster, which is growth by stages. The 'inexpensive' option raises cost, and the text mentions only time and the sequence of courses.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2E.passage: Limewash is slaked lime thinned with water and brushed on in coats so thin that the wall shows through the first of them. It shuts nothing in: damp reaching the face of a limewashed wall passes out through the coating and dries, so no water is trapped behind a skin. A fresh coat costs the price of the lime and a morning of somebody's time. Its virtue is not that it lasts but that it is so easily _____.
RW_M2E.why: The passage contrasts durability with the cheap yearly recoating the material invites, so what is being praised is the ease of putting it on again. The 'removed' option describes taking the coating off, which the text never treats as an advantage or even mentions.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2E.passage: A thatched roof is not sealed. Water reed is laid in overlapping courses with the cut butts facing outward, and rain that strikes the surface runs down the outside of the stems and off the eaves without passing more than a few centimetres into the coat. The pitch matters more than the depth, because a shallow roof lets the water travel along the stems instead of down them: the covering works by _____ the rain rather than by blocking it.
RW_M2E.why: The passage says the water runs down the outside and off the eaves without penetrating, which is a matter of directing it away. The 'absorbing' option describes taking the water in, and the text states that it barely enters the coat at all.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2E.passage: A hide is moved through a series of pits, each holding a stronger liquor of crushed oak bark than the last, and a year may pass before it comes out. A tanner who hurries the sequence fixes the outer faces of the hide before the liquor has reached the middle, and the leather cracks along the fold. The slowness of the older pits was therefore _____ rather than a mark of an industry that had not yet been improved.
RW_M2E.why: The passage explains what goes wrong when the sequence is hurried, which makes the pace a choice serving a purpose. The 'customary' option says only that the practice was habitual, which is exactly the reading the sentence sets aside.

RW_M2E.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “charge” most nearly mean?
RW_M2E.passage: A lime kiln is loaded from the top in alternating layers: a bed of coal, then broken limestone, then coal again, until the shaft is full. The burner draws quicklime from the grate at the bottom as the column settles and adds another <u>charge</u> at the top, so that the kiln runs for months without being emptied or allowed to cool.
RW_M2E.why: The word names the thing added at the top of a shaft that is drawn off at the bottom, which is a measured load of fuel and stone. The 'fee demanded' sense is the commercial one, and nothing in the passage concerns payment.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
RW_M2E.passage: Stones grind the whole grain at once, so the oil of the germ is smeared through the meal and the flour turns rancid within weeks. <u>Rollers set in pairs and turned at different speeds shear each grain open instead of crushing it, so that bran and germ come away in flakes large enough to be sifted out whole.</u> The flour that resulted was white, kept for months and could be sent anywhere, and the country mills lost the trade within a generation.
RW_M2E.why: The underlined sentence describes the shearing action that separates bran and germ, and the closing sentence lists the keeping quality and whiteness that follow from that separation. The loss of trade is stated in the final sentence, not in the underlined one.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It identifies the change in method that accounts for the qualities described afterwards.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It concedes that stone-ground flour had advantages the new method lacked.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It explains why the germ of the grain contains oil.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It estimates how quickly the country mills lost their trade.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
RW_M2E.passage: A plank walkway laid across a reed swamp about 3800 BCE survives beneath a Somerset peat field. <u>Its builders drove pairs of pegs into the swamp in a long crossed line, dropped a rail into the notch where each pair crossed, and pegged the planks down onto the rail.</u> Nothing in the structure rested on the surface itself. The result carried people in single file above ground that would not have held a standing adult.
RW_M2E.why: The underlined sentence describes how the pegs, rail and planks were assembled, and the two sentences after it state what that assembly achieved: a load carried clear of unbearing ground. The date appears in the opening sentence rather than in the underlined one.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It establishes the date at which the walkway was built.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It accounts for the survival of the timbers in the peat.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It compares the walkway with roads built later in the same region.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It sets out the arrangement whose purpose the rest of the text explains.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
RW_M2E.passage: The signs of the earliest alphabet are pictures: an ox head, a house, a door. Each sign stands not for the thing drawn but for the sound that opens the word naming it, so the ox head writes the first sound of the word for ox. Twenty-odd signs used this way covered a language that would have needed several hundred to be written word by word, and a list that short could be learned in days by people who were not scribes by trade.
RW_M2E.why: The text explains the sound-for-picture principle and then draws the consequence: a couple of dozen signs in place of several hundred, learnable outside the scribal trade. The option about ease of drawing offers a reason for the choice of pictures that the passage never gives.

choices.label: A
choices.content: An alphabet of twenty-odd signs cannot represent every sound of a language.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Letting each picture stand for the first sound of its own name cut writing down to a couple of dozen signs.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The pictures were chosen because they were the easiest shapes to draw.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Scribes resisted the new signs because the older system suited them better.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
RW_M2E.passage: An acre began as a day's work rather than a quantity of ground: the strip a man with a yoke of oxen could plough between morning and evening. Its size therefore moved with the soil, and a heavy clay acre was a good deal smaller than an acre of light loam. The unit told a farmer the one thing he needed, which was how long a field would take him. It told a purchaser at a distance nothing whatever about how much ground he was buying.
RW_M2E.why: The text derives the acre from a day at the plough, shows its area shifting with the soil, and then separates what it tells the farmer from what it fails to tell a distant buyer. The option about productivity treats the varying size as a difference between ploughmen, when the passage attributes it to the ground.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The acre was abandoned once oxen were replaced by horses at the plough.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Farmers preferred light loam because it could be ploughed into larger fields.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A unit defined by a day's labour reported effort accurately and area only loosely.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Ploughmen working heavy clay were less productive than those working light loam.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
RW_M2E.passage:
A commission of 1826 collected the bushel measures actually in use in four market towns, had each of them filled with water and weighed, and set the result against the Winchester standard of 35.2 litres.
TownCapacity of local bushel (litres)
Barrowden37.7
Chettle33.1
Denton35.2
Elsdon40.0
Three of the four towns were using a measure that differed from the standard, and the measure furthest from it was the one in use at _____
RW_M2E.why: The difference of 4.8 litres at 40.0 is larger than the differences of 2.5 and 2.1 litres recorded at the other two towns that departed from the standard. The town whose bushel held exactly 35.2 litres is the one that matched the standard, so it cannot be the furthest from it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Chettle, whose bushel of 33.1 litres fell short of the standard by 2.1 litres.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Barrowden, whose bushel of 37.7 litres exceeded the standard by 2.5 litres.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Denton, whose bushel held exactly 35.2 litres.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Elsdon, whose bushel of 40.0 litres exceeded the standard by 4.8 litres.

RW_M2E.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Achebe's argument?
RW_M2E.passage: In a few arable fields a root disease that is present in the soil nevertheless fails to damage the crop, and the fields keep this property for decades. Soil scientist Wren Achebe argues that the suppression is the work of living organisms in the soil rather than of its chemistry.
RW_M2E.why: Heat destroys organisms but leaves the mineral chemistry, and a small untreated inoculum restoring the effect is what a living, self-multiplying agent does and a chemical property does not. The finding about organic matter records a difference between the soils without showing that anything alive is responsible.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Heating a suppressive soil destroys the suppression, and mixing one part of untreated soil into fifty parts of the heated soil restores it.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Suppressive fields hold more organic matter than neighbouring fields that lack the property.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The disease damages crops most severely in warm, wet seasons.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Suppressive soils have been recorded on several continents and in several soil types.

RW_M2E.stem: Which quotation from the notebook most effectively illustrates Rask's claim?
RW_M2E.passage: Between 1936 and 1939 an amateur excavator kept a notebook while a ditch was deepened along the edge of a fen, where rows of oak piles kept appearing in the cut. Archaeologist Nils Rask argues that the notebook shows its author satisfying himself that the piles were the footings of a built structure some two years before he could persuade anyone else of it.
RW_M2E.why: The quotation reasons from the regular spacing of the piles to a structure deliberately raised above the water, which is the conclusion the claim says he had reached early. The quotation about sawing two piles through records an action taken without saying what the excavator made of them.

choices.label: A
choices.content: “They stand four abreast and at even spacing, and no flood I can picture would set them so; I take them for the footings of something raised above the water.”

choices.label: B
choices.content: “The ditch was opened to a depth of five feet and the spoil laid along the western bank.”

choices.label: C
choices.content: “Mr Ridley of the Manor Farm allows that we may work the field until Michaelmas next year.”

choices.label: D
choices.content: “Two of the piles were sawn through at the waterline and the sections carried to the county museum.”

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2E.passage: Egyptian inscriptions run left to right in some places and right to left in others, and a single wall may carry lines of both kinds. The signs themselves settle the question: the human and animal figures always face towards the start of the line, so a row of owls and seated men looking leftward is to be read from the left. A reader who has never seen a particular inscription before can therefore _____
RW_M2E.why: The passage gives one rule, that the figures look towards the beginning, and that rule supplies exactly one thing: the end at which a line starts. The option about translating without the language goes far beyond a rule that fixes direction and nothing else.

choices.label: A
choices.content: translate the inscription without knowing anything of the language it records.

choices.label: B
choices.content: date the inscription by the direction in which its lines were cut.

choices.label: C
choices.content: tell which of the figures the inscription was composed to honour.

choices.label: D
choices.content: work out which end of each line to begin at from the direction the figures face.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2E.passage: Tannin enters a hide slowly, working inward from both faces at once, and a hide lifted too early looks finished from the outside. A tanner therefore cuts a narrow strip from the edge of a hide and examines the cut end: where the liquor has done its work the section is brown throughout, and where it has not an untanned core shows as a pale line down the middle. A pale line in the sample tells the tanner that _____
RW_M2E.why: The passage states that the pale core is untanned material and that tannin works inward from both faces, so a pale middle means the process is unfinished rather than spoiled. The option about scorching would describe damage at the surfaces, and it is the surfaces that the passage says are already brown.

choices.label: A
choices.content: the hide was cut from an animal too young to yield usable leather.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the sample was taken from the wrong part of the hide and must be cut again.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the hide must go back into the pits, since the liquor has not yet reached its centre.

choices.label: D
choices.content: the liquor was too strong and has scorched the outer faces of the hide.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: The weir at the mill stood two metres high and was cut down to a low sill in 2011, the first of eleven on the river to be lowered. Salmon now pass the site at almost any state of the flow, and redds have been counted every spring since in the Kirkby reach above it, four miles of clean _____ had held no spawning fish since the weir was raised in the 1830s.
RW_M2E.why: The reach has already been named and measured, so the clause about spawning fish adds information rather than picking out which gravel is meant, and a comma marks it off. A semicolon or a colon would need a complete statement after it, and a clause opening with 'which' is not one.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: A tanner judges a pit by smell and by the feel of the hide rather than by any measurement. The hides that come out of the strongest _____ enough to stand on edge by themselves, and they have to be worked with oil and a slicker before they will bend around a last.
RW_M2E.why: The words naming which hides are meant belong to the subject and must not be cut off from the verb that follows them. Every other arrangement drops a comma between the subject and its verb, or between the verb and what completes it.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: A survey of a saltmarsh follows the creeks before it records anything else, because the creeks govern the rest. Their branching pattern settles the one question that matters to every plant growing on the _____ long each patch of ground lies under salt water on each tide.
RW_M2E.why: What follows the blank is not a complete statement but the content of the question just mentioned, and a colon is the mark that introduces it. A semicolon requires a complete statement on both sides, and a comma is too weak to carry the announcement.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: Rain moving down through the sandy floor of a conifer wood picks up iron and aluminium from the top of the profile and drops them again a hand's breadth lower. Because the same water carries the colour down with _____ podzol shows a bleached grey band lying directly above a rust-coloured one.
RW_M2E.why: The introductory clause beginning with 'because' has to be closed with a comma before the main statement starts. A semicolon or colon would require a complete statement in front of it, and the clause is not one.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: The pyramid was enlarged five times, each new shell built over the last, and the tunnels driven into the mound in the 1930s found the earlier stairways still standing inside it. The two archaeologists who worked on the tunnels disagreed for years about the date of the earliest of them. The report that finally settled the sequence was written jointly by the field director and _____.
RW_M2E.why: The pronoun is one of two objects of the preposition 'by', so it takes the object form. The subject form would be required only if the pronoun were doing the writing rather than being named after 'by'.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: The last of the windpumps on this level was taken down in 1938 and sold for its timber, and the land it once drained lies well below the river that carries the water away. Ever since that winter the district _____ dry by three diesel pumps and a tidal sluice at the outfall.
RW_M2E.why: The stretch of time runs from a point in the past up to the present, which is what the present perfect marks. The simple past would close the period off in 1938, and the past perfect would put the pumping before some other past event that the sentence never supplies.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2E.passage: The parish had specified a lime mortar for the repair of the church, on the advice of an architect who had seen what cement does to soft stone. The masons brought in for the work had all been trained on cement and had never mixed lime in their lives. _____ first batch set so slowly that the scaffold had to stand for a month while it hardened.
RW_M2E.why: The batch belongs to more than one mason, so the plural noun takes an apostrophe after the final letter. The singular possessive would point at one worker, and the passage has named several.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2E.passage: A knot feeding on a mudflat swallows small shellfish whole and grinds them in a muscular gizzard that grows heavier the harder the shells it works on. That same organ shrinks to a fraction of its weight in the days before a long flight, and it takes several days to rebuild afterwards. _____ the first food a bird takes at the far end of its journey tends to be soft-bodied worms rather than shellfish.
RW_M2E.why: A gizzard that has shrunk and has not yet been rebuilt cannot grind shells, so the choice of soft prey on arrival follows from what the previous sentence describes. A concession would require the last sentence to work against that, and it agrees with it.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2E.passage: Water travels through a heavy clay only as fast as the cracks and worm channels in it allow, and a pipe drain laid in such a soil can run dry while the field a metre above it stands waterlogged. Drainers pull a bullet-shaped mole through the clay at half the depth of the pipe, splitting the ground into fissures that lead down to it. _____ the water reaches the pipe by a route the soil could not have provided for itself.
RW_M2E.why: The fissures split into the clay are what carry the water down to a pipe it could not otherwise reach, so the last sentence states the outcome of the operation described before it. A concession would require that sentence to work against the moling, and it reports its effect.

RW_M2E.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2E.passage: Water reed cut in winter stands almost upright in a roof and can last sixty years before it is stripped. Long straw is softer, lies flatter and is generally renewed after twenty-five. _____ a straw roof is cheaper to lay and can be patched in a morning where a gale has lifted it.
RW_M2E.why: The final sentence gives straw an advantage that stands against the shorter life just reported for it, so the transition concedes rather than concludes. A consequence relation would make cheap patching follow from the shorter life, which it does not.

RW_M2E.stem: The student wants to explain how one piece of ground could yield two things at once. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2E.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A pollard is a tree cut back to a permanent trunk two or three metres above the ground.
  • The height of the cut puts the regrowth out of reach of cattle and deer.
  • Wood pasture carries grazing animals and a wood crop on the same ground.
  • A tree that is cut in this way regularly can go on producing for several centuries.
  • The cut poles were used for fuel, fencing and tool handles.
RW_M2E.why: The goal asks how one acre produced both, and only the choice tying the height of the cut to the protection of the regrowth explains how the grazing and the wood crop coexist. The note about several centuries of production reports longevity, which is a separate benefit.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A tree cut in this way regularly can go on producing for several centuries.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A pollard is a tree cut back to a permanent trunk above the ground.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The cut poles were used for fuel, fencing and tool handles.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Cutting above the height cattle and deer can reach keeps the regrowth safe from them, so the same ground carries grazing animals and a wood crop together.

RW_M2E.stem: The student wants to explain why the ridge is dealt with separately from the rest of the roof. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2E.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The ridge of a thatched roof takes more weather than the slopes below it.
  • A ridge is renewed every ten to fifteen years.
  • A full re-coat of the slopes is needed only every twenty-five to sixty years, depending on the material.
  • Re-ridging requires a few days of work and one bundle of sedge in ten of the coat.
  • The ridge is fixed with hazel spars and can be stripped without disturbing the coat beneath it.
RW_M2E.why: The goal asks why the ridge is treated on its own, and only the choice pairing its faster wear with the fact that it comes off without touching the coat gives the reason. The interval of ten to fifteen years states how often the work is done without saying why it is done separately.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Because the ridge wears out several times over during the life of the coat and can be stripped without disturbing it, it is renewed on its own in a few days.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Re-ridging requires one bundle of sedge in every ten of the coat.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The ridge of a thatched roof takes more weather than the slopes below it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A ridge is renewed every ten to fifteen years.

RW_M2E.stem: The student wants to explain why a millwright would go to the expense of digging a leat. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2E.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • An undershot wheel is turned by water striking the paddles at the bottom of the wheel.
  • An overshot wheel is turned by the weight of water carried down in buckets from the top.
  • An overshot wheel needs a head of water at least as high as the wheel itself.
  • Building a leat along the contour can carry water from far upstream to the top of a wheel.
  • For the same flow, an overshot wheel yields roughly twice the power of an undershot one.
RW_M2E.why: The goal asks what justifies the cost of the channel, and only the choice linking the head the leat provides to the doubled power gives a reason. Stating that a leat can carry water from upstream describes what it does without saying what is gained by it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Building a leat along the contour can carry water from far upstream.

choices.label: B
choices.content: An undershot wheel is turned by water striking its paddles at the bottom.

choices.label: C
choices.content: A leat carried along the contour delivers water at the height an overshot wheel needs, and such a wheel yields about twice the power of an undershot one on the same flow.

choices.label: D
choices.content: An overshot wheel is turned by the weight of water carried down in buckets.

RW_M2H.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “standard” most nearly mean?
RW_M2H.passage: The bronze yard kept at the Exchequer was not a description of a length; it was the length. Nothing defined it and nothing could correct it, because there was no longer measure behind it to appeal to. Every yard in the kingdom descended from that one bar, so a dispute about a yard could in principle be settled by fetching the <u>standard</u> out and laying the two side by side.
RW_M2H.why: The passage describes a physical bar that copies are laid against and derived from, so the word names that object rather than any abstract measure. The 'level of quality expected' sense is the common modern one and cannot be fetched and compared, which the sentence requires.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2H.passage: The face of a millstone is not flat. Shallow furrows are cut from the centre outward in groups, and the flat lands between them are pitted with fine tooling. Grain travelling out between the stones is caught by the edges where furrow meets land and is cut rather than crushed, and the furrows carry the meal and the air that cools it towards the rim. A stone left smooth heats the flour and spoils it, so the pattern is strictly _____.
RW_M2H.why: Every feature of the pattern is given a job in the sentences before the blank, and the consequence of leaving it off is a spoiled product. The 'ornamental' option is the reading the passage rules out, since nothing about the dressing is described as being for show.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2H.passage: Elvers reaching the foot of a weir will climb anything they can grip, even a wetted wall, but they cannot cross a smooth vertical face with water sheeting down it. A shallow channel lined with stiff bristles and fed with a trickle of water gives them purchase for the whole height of the structure. The fitting costs little and moves nothing, yet it renders a barrier that had been _____ merely inconvenient.
RW_M2H.why: The passage says the elvers cannot cross the smooth face at all and then describes a fitting that lets them up it, so the barrier's former condition was total exclusion. The 'expensive' option refers to cost, which the sentence attaches to the fitting rather than to the weir.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2H.passage: A charcoal burner stacks cordwood into a dome, covers it with earth and dust, and lights it from a shaft down the middle. Air must reach the wood, or the fire goes out and the stack is wasted; too much air and the wood burns away to ash instead of charring. The burner opens one small vent and stops another through the night, so the making of charcoal is less an act of lighting a fire than a matter of keeping it _____.
RW_M2H.why: The passage sets the danger of too much air against the danger of none and describes the burner rationing air vent by vent, so the fire is kept deliberately short of it. The 'sheltered' option describes protection from the weather, which the earth covering is never said to provide.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
RW_M2H.passage: Fibres are twisted one way into yarns, the yarns are twisted the opposite way into strands, and the strands are twisted back the first way into rope. Each layer is trying to unwind itself and is prevented by the layer around it, which is winding the other way. Cut the rope and the end will fray, but along its length the opposed twists hold one another in _____.
RW_M2H.why: The passage describes two opposed tendencies that cancel each other out along the rope's length, which is a balance of forces. The 'sequence' option describes an order in time, and the twists are acting against each other at the same moment rather than one after another.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
RW_M2H.passage: Six species of wader feed on one mudflat at the same tide. Their bills run from the two-centimetre probe of a stint to the twelve-centimetre curve of a curlew, and the animals buried in the mud are arranged by depth: small snails and thin worms near the surface, thick worms and burrowing crabs well below. Records of what each species swallows show almost no overlap at all between the shortest bills and the longest.
RW_M2H.why: The text pairs a range of bill lengths with prey sorted by depth and closes on the absence of overlap in what the birds eat, which is a division of one feeding ground. The option about curlews driving other birds away describes a conflict the text never reports.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To explain how species feeding on the same ground take different prey from it.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To argue that curlews drive smaller waders off the flats they share.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To describe how the animals buried in a mudflat construct their burrows.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To establish which of the six species is the most numerous on the flat.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
RW_M2H.passage: <u>A Maya vault is built by setting each course of stone a little further out than the course below until the two sides almost meet, and closing the gap with a capstone.</u> Nothing in the structure carries a load sideways, so the walls must be thick enough to hold the overhang up by sheer weight. Rooms roofed in this way are narrow, tall and dark, and widening a room by a metre costs far more than a metre of extra masonry.
RW_M2H.why: The underlined sentence sets out the stepped-course method, and everything after it follows from that method: no sideways thrust, thick walls, narrow rooms, rising cost with width. No arch of any other tradition is mentioned anywhere in the text.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It explains why the capstone is the heaviest element in the roof.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It states how tall the rooms roofed in this way could be made.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It describes the construction whose consequences the rest of the text traces.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It contrasts the Maya vault with the arch used in other building traditions.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
RW_M2H.passage: A lime mortar is weaker than the brick or stone it beds, and that is the point of it. As a wall moves, the fine cracks open along the joints rather than through the units, and a joint is the one part of a wall a mason can rake out and replace. A cement mortar is much stronger and much stiffer, and in a wall of soft brick the crack runs through the brick instead. Repointing an old soft wall in cement can leave it worse than it was.
RW_M2H.why: The text explains that the weaker material concentrates cracking in the replaceable joints and that a stiffer mortar sends the cracking into the brick instead. The option saying cement cracks more readily reverses the passage, which describes cement as the stronger material and the brick as the part that fails.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Cement mortar cracks more readily than lime mortar does.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Soft bricks should be replaced with harder ones before a wall is repointed.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The chief advantage of lime mortar is that it costs less than cement.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Mortar weaker than the masonry sends damage into the joints, where it can be repaired, which is why cement can harm a soft old wall.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
RW_M2H.passage: Two constructions account for nearly every basket ever made. In the first, a bundle of grass or straw is wound in a rising spiral and each turn is stitched to the one below it, so the wall grows by sewing. In the second, stout rods are set upright as a framework and finer rods are woven in and out between them, so the wall grows by weaving. The first needs a needle and almost no strength; the second needs rods that bend without cracking and a maker who can hold them under strain.
RW_M2H.why: The text describes one wall grown by stitching and another grown by weaving, then pairs each with what it demands: a needle in one case, pliable rods and strength in the other. The comparison of strength between the two kinds of basket is never made in the passage.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Both methods were developed in order to make use of grass and straw.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Basketmakers generally learn the woven method before attempting the coiled one.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The two methods build a wall in different ways and therefore ask different things of the maker's material and tools.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Coiled baskets are stronger than woven ones and last considerably longer.

RW_M2H.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sørensen's argument?
RW_M2H.passage: Salmon hatched in a small tributary return years later to the same tributary, choosing correctly at every fork on the way up. Biologist Ingrid Sørensen argues that the fish make those choices by smell, having learned the odour of their own stream before they went to sea.
RW_M2H.why: Blocking the sense of smell and finding that the choice at the fork becomes random is what distinguishes an odour cue from any other, since everything else about the fish is unchanged. The finding about a one-degree difference in temperature names an alternative cue rather than supporting the one being argued for.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Young salmon spend between one and three years in fresh water before going to sea.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The two branches of the confluence differ in temperature by about one degree in summer.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Adults whose nostrils were plugged turned into the two branches of a confluence at random, while untagged fish from the same run turned overwhelmingly into their natal branch.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Salmon return to the river in greater numbers in years when the autumn flow is high.

RW_M2H.stem: Which quotation from the letter book most effectively illustrates Larkin's claim?
RW_M2H.passage: The letter book of a Munster tannery covers the years 1783 to 1791, and its entries record purchases, wages and the state of the pits alongside the partners' correspondence with their agents in Cork and Bristol. Historian Aoife Larkin argues that what governed the firm's output in those years was its supply of oak bark rather than its supply of hides.
RW_M2H.why: The quotation sets the ready availability of hides against bark as the thing that decides how many pits can be worked, which is the comparison the claim rests on. The quotation about the price of sole leather concerns what the product fetches rather than what limits how much of it the tannery can make.

choices.label: A
choices.content: “We have taken on two men for the beam house and shall want a third before spring.”

choices.label: B
choices.content: “Hides we may have out of Cork whenever we send for them; it is the bark that settles how many pits we dare lay down.”

choices.label: C
choices.content: “The new pits behind the drying loft were finished at Michaelmas and are of the same depth as the old.”

choices.label: D
choices.content: “Sole leather is fetching a better price this season than at any time since the war.”

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
RW_M2H.passage:
Knots feeding on an estuary before their northward flight are caught, weighed and released. A team recorded the mean mass of the birds caught in the week of their arrival and again in the week before they left, at four estuaries in the same spring.
EstuaryMean mass on arrival (g)Mean mass before departure (g)
Dornoch130205
Solway128196
Ribble126171
Wash133188
The birds gained mass at every estuary in the study, and the largest gain was recorded at _____
RW_M2H.why: The gain of 75 grams from 130 to 205 is larger than the gains of 68, 55 and 45 grams recorded at the other three estuaries. The entry reporting 133 grams on arrival gives the heaviest arrival mass rather than the largest gain, and its gain of 55 grams is among the smaller ones.

choices.label: A
choices.content: the Solway, where the birds weighed a mean of 196 grams before departure.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Dornoch, where a mean of 130 grams on arrival had become 205 grams before departure.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the Wash, where the birds arrived at a mean of 133 grams.

choices.label: D
choices.content: the Ribble, where a mean of 126 grams on arrival had become 171 grams before departure.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2H.passage: A tracking device recovered from a bar-tailed godwit recorded a departure from an Alaskan estuary and a landfall in New Zealand eight days later, with no stop anywhere in between. Before leaving, the bird had roughly doubled its lean weight in fat, and the organs it uses to digest food had shrunk to a fraction of their usual size. Taken together, these observations indicate that the bird _____
RW_M2H.why: A doubled fat load and a digestive system reduced to a fraction of its working size describe a bird equipped to burn stores and not to process food, over a flight with no landfall. The option about feeding at sea contradicts the shrunken digestive organs, which are what makes feeding impossible.

choices.label: A
choices.content: would have been unable to complete the flight without a following wind.

choices.label: B
choices.content: had to carry the whole of its fuel from the start, being in no condition to feed on the way.

choices.label: C
choices.content: fed on small animals taken from the surface of the sea during the crossing.

choices.label: D
choices.content: made the crossing more slowly than a bird that had not laid down fat.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
RW_M2H.passage: When a peat fen is drained the peat dries, shrinks and wastes away as air reaches it. In 1851 an iron column was driven down through the peat of one such fen until it rested on the clay beneath, and its top was set flush with the surface of the field. The column has not been touched since, and its top now stands more than three metres above the ground around it. The column therefore serves as _____
RW_M2H.why: The column is fixed on the clay and was set level with the ground, so the gap that has opened between its top and the field can only be ground that has gone. The option about the clay being pushed upward would require the column to have risen, which the passage rules out by saying it has not moved.

choices.label: A
choices.content: a measure of how far the surface of the fen has fallen since the drainage.

choices.label: B
choices.content: evidence that the clay beneath the peat has been pushed slowly upward.

choices.label: C
choices.content: a record of the height reached by the water in the drain beside it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: proof that the wasting of the peat has now come to an end.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: A drained catchment can be held no lower than the level to which its water can be lifted or run away. Gravity does the whole of the work wherever the outfall lies below the fields it serves _____ most of this fen now lies below the river it drains into, and the difference has to be made up by pumping.
RW_M2H.why: Two complete statements meet at the blank, and the connecting adverb does not join them, so a semicolon is needed in front of it. A comma there leaves the two statements spliced, and a colon would announce an explanation rather than a contrast.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: A cruck frame is cut from a single curved tree split down its length, so the two blades of each pair are mirror images and meet at the ridge without any fitting. The frames were reared one after another and pegged together along the length of the building _____ walls were built around them afterwards and carry no part of the roof at all.
RW_M2H.why: Two complete statements are joined by a coordinating conjunction, which takes a comma in front of it. Dropping the comma runs the two statements together, and putting the comma after the conjunction cuts it off from the clause it introduces.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: A patent sail carries rows of hinged shutters linked by a rod that runs the length of the whip, and a weight hung on the striking rod sets the pressure at which they fly open. The gear does the one thing no earlier sail could _____ the gusts without the miller stopping the mill, climbing out and reefing cloth on each of the four sails in turn.
RW_M2H.why: What follows the blank explains the claim made before it, and a colon is the mark that introduces an explanation of that kind. The comma produces a splice between two complete statements, and a colon is never followed by a coordinating conjunction.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: Quicklime drawn from the kiln is not yet mortar. Water poured onto it releases enough heat to boil the slurry, and the lumps fall apart into a putty that goes on softening for months afterwards. A mason working to a lime specification plans for the delay and slakes the lime long before the wall is _____ mixed the same week is gritty, harsh under the trowel and slow to set.
RW_M2H.why: Two complete statements stand on either side of the blank with no conjunction between them, which is what the semicolon is for. The comma alone splices them together, and a colon does not take a conjunction after it.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: A round basket starts from a slath: short rods split down the middle, threaded through one another at right angles and then opened out like the spokes of a wheel. Longer rods are worked in around them until the base is closed. Bent up out of the finished base and held under strain until the first rows of weaving lock them in position, _____
RW_M2H.why: The opening phrase describes whatever has been bent up and held under strain, and only the stakes can be, so the stakes have to be the subject of the clause that follows. Each of the other versions puts the shape, or the taking of it, in that position, and neither can be bent up out of a basket base.

choices.label: A
choices.content: the stakes take the shape that the whole basket will keep.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the shape that the whole basket will keep is taken by the stakes.

choices.label: C
choices.content: there is a shape taken by the stakes that the whole basket keeps.

choices.label: D
choices.content: taking the shape the whole basket keeps is what the stakes do.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: The commission wrote to every market town in the kingdom, asked what measures were in daily use there, and printed the returns without amending them. Some towns sent in three or four measures for different commodities. The number of distinct local bushels reported to it in 1826 _____ greater than the number of counties that answered at all.
RW_M2H.why: The subject is 'the number', which is singular however many things are being counted. The plural verbs agree with 'bushels', a noun that sits inside a phrase modifying the subject.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
RW_M2H.passage: Eleven weirs stand between the tide and the headwaters of this river, and each of them now carries a bristle-lined channel up which the young eels can climb. Every pass is inspected in April, before the elvers arrive in numbers. The bristles are lifted out and washed, and any pass whose channel has silted up has _____ trickle of water restored before the run begins.
RW_M2H.why: The pronoun stands for a single pass and shows possession, which is the form without an apostrophe. The contracted form means 'it is', and the plural would disagree with the singular 'any pass'.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: The earliest Greek inscriptions run from right to left, the direction of the Phoenician script they were adapted from. Others run in alternating directions, turning at the end of each line the way a plough turns at the end of a furrow. _____ the left-to-right arrangement that became standard was for well over a century only one option among several.
RW_M2H.why: The final sentence gathers the varied directions just listed into a single statement about them, which is a summary rather than a new case. A contrast would set the last sentence against the examples, and it instead sums them up.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: Sole leather is tanned slowly and left thick and firm, so that it wears down under the foot instead of stretching out of shape. _____ the leather of an upper is curried with oils and tallow until it is soft enough to fold around the foot at every step.
RW_M2H.why: The two sentences set two leathers against each other, one made firm and the other made supple, so the transition marks the opposition. A consequence relation would require the second leather to follow from the first, and it does not.

RW_M2H.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
RW_M2H.passage: A stack of green wood loses well over half its weight when it is charred, and what remains burns hotter than the wood it came from. _____ charcoal was made in the wood where the timber grew and carried out on horseback, rather than the timber being carted whole to the town.
RW_M2H.why: The weight lost in charring is the reason for burning the wood where it stood and moving only the product, so the second sentence states a consequence of the first. A contrast would require the second sentence to cut against the first, which it does not.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain how blocking the ditches changes what a drained bog does. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Peat forms only while the ground stays waterlogged, and it wastes away once air reaches it.
  • A drained peat field loses several millimetres of its surface every year.
  • Blocking the ditches on a drained bog raises the water table back to within a few centimetres of the surface.
  • Sphagnum moss returns to the wetted surface within a few seasons.
  • Gas measurements on rewetted bogs record far less carbon dioxide leaving the ground than before the ditches were blocked.
RW_M2H.why: The goal asks what the blocking changes, and only the choice joining the raised water table to the fall in carbon dioxide leaving the ground states the change. The return of the moss reports a further effect without connecting it to what the ditch blocking did.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Blocking the ditches raises the water table to within a few centimetres of the surface, and gas measurements then record far less carbon dioxide leaving the ground.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A drained peat field loses several millimetres of its surface every year.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Peat forms only while the ground stays waterlogged.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Sphagnum moss returns to a rewetted surface within a few seasons.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain why parchment is not a kind of leather. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Tanning binds tannin into the fibres of a hide, and a tanned hide never returns to its raw state.
  • Parchment is made by liming a skin, scraping it and drying it under tension; no tannin is used at all.
  • Parchment that is wetted relaxes, shrinks and cockles as it dries again.
  • A tanned hide that is wetted dries flat and unchanged.
  • Parchment and leather are both made from animal skin.
RW_M2H.why: The goal asks for the distinction, and only the choice contrasting the tension-dried, tannin-free sheet with the tanned hide's behaviour when wetted supplies one. Noting that both are made from skin gives what the two have in common, which is the opposite of what the goal asks for.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Parchment and leather are both made from animal skin.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Parchment is dried under tension without tannin, so wetting relaxes and cockles it, whereas a tanned hide dries flat and unchanged.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Parchment is made by liming a skin and then scraping it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A tanned hide never returns to its raw state once the tannin is in the fibres.

RW_M2H.stem: The student wants to explain how breaching the old wall changed the life of the site. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
RW_M2H.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A sea wall built across an estuary in 1850 cut off two hundred hectares of grazing from the tide.
  • The marsh in front of the wall narrowed as the sea rose against it.
  • A new wall was built inland in 2002 and the old one was breached.
  • Glasswort colonised the bare mud behind the breach within two seasons.
  • Counts of feeding waders on the site rose sharply in the years after the breach.
RW_M2H.why: The goal asks what the breach did to the living community, and only the choice pairing the colonising plants with the rise in feeding waders reports it. Building the new wall inland describes the engineering step without any consequence for what lives there.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Letting the tide back through the breach allowed glasswort to colonise the bare mud within two seasons, and counts of feeding waders on the site rose sharply afterwards.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A new wall was built further inland in 2002.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The marsh in front of the old wall narrowed as the sea rose against it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A sea wall built across the estuary in 1850 cut off two hundred hectares from the tide.

MATH_M1.stem: A peat cutter worked the first 3 hours of the day at 240 turves an hour and then, as the bank grew wetter, at 180 turves an hour for the rest of the day. By the end of the day 1,440 turves had been cut. For how many hours did the cutter work altogether?
MATH_M1.check: The first 3 hours yield 720 turves, so 180h = 720 more takes h = 4 further hours, and 3 + 4 = 7 hours in all.

MATH_M1.stem: In a charcoal burner's stack the rings of billets are counted upward from the ground, and the number of billets falls by the same amount from each ring to the next. The third ring holds 70 billets and the eighth ring holds 40 billets. How many billets does the twelfth ring hold?
MATH_M1.check: The fall per ring is (40-70)/(8-3) = -6 billets, so the twelfth ring holds 70 - 6(12-3) = 16.

MATH_M1.stem: A tannery buys shredded oak bark by the sack. One merchant charges a delivery fee of $65 and then $18 for each sack; a second merchant charges no delivery fee but $23 for each sack. For one particular order the two merchants would charge exactly the same amount. What is that amount?

A grazier holds a licence for a saltmarsh of 46 hectares which permits at most 2.5 ewes per hectare, and under the licence each lamb counts as half a ewe. The grazier already runs 74 ewes on the marsh. What is the greatest number of lambs the grazier may add without breaking the licence?
MATH_M1.check: The licence allows 46(2.5) = 115 ewes, and 74 + 0.5L <= 115 gives L <= 82.

MATH_M1.stem: An eel fisher sets 56 traps in all, spread over the upper, middle and lower reaches of a river. The middle reach holds 3 times as many traps as the upper reach, and the lower reach holds 6 more traps than the upper reach. How many traps are set in the lower reach?
MATH_M1.check: With u traps in the upper reach, u + 3u + (u+6) = 56 gives u = 10, so the lower reach holds 16.

MATH_M1.stem: A tannery bought 40 sacks of coarse bark at $12 a sack and a number of sacks of fine bark at $20 a sack. Taking every sack bought together, the average cost worked out at $15 a sack. How many sacks of fine bark did the tannery buy?

The discharge through a sluice gate is a linear function of the head of water standing behind it. The table gives two readings taken by the keeper.
Head of water (metres)Discharge (cubic metres per second)
0.53.4
2.07.0
What head of water, in metres, does this relationship give for a discharge of 10.6 cubic metres per second?
MATH_M1.check: The rate is (7.0-3.4)/(2.0-0.5) = 2.4 and the discharge at zero head is 3.4 - 0.5(2.4) = 2.2, so 2.4H + 2.2 = 10.6 gives H = 3.5.

MATH_M1.stem: A charcoal burner models the mass of charcoal lost to the flue, in kilograms, as \(L(x)=2x^{2}-20x+63\), where x is the number of hours the stack has been alight. Which expression is equivalent to \(L(x)\) and shows the least possible loss as a constant?
MATH_M1.check: Taking 2 out of the first two terms gives 2(x-5)^2 - 50 + 63, which is 2(x-5)^2 + 13.

MATH_M1.stem: The number of elvers passing an eel weir in a week is modelled by \(N(w)=N_{0}b^{w}\), where w is the number of the week and \(N_{0}\) and b are constants. The model gives 180 elvers in week 2 and 1,440 elvers in week 5. How many elvers does the model give for week 4?
MATH_M1.check: Three weeks multiply the count by 1,440/180 = 8, so b = 2, and week 4 is 1,440/2 = 720.

MATH_M1.stem: The floor of a sluice channel is modelled in the xy-plane by the curve \(y=x^{2}-8x+20\), and the surface of the water is modelled by the line y=5. The line meets the curve at two points. What is the distance between those two points?
MATH_M1.check: x^2 - 8x + 20 = 5 gives x = 3 and x = 5, and the two points share the same y, so they are 2 apart.

MATH_M1.stem: A tannery's drum controller turns a dial reading x into a drum speed \(f(x)=\frac{2x+k}{x-3}\), where k is a constant and \(x>3\). A dial reading of 5 gives a speed of 7. What speed does a dial reading of 4 give?

A tannery's cutting plan gives the area of a hide panel, in square decimetres, as \((3x+m)(2x-5)\), where m is a constant. The same area is also given by \(6x^{2}-9x-15\) for every value of x. What is the value of m?
MATH_M1.check: Expanding gives 6x^2 + (2m-15)x - 5m, so 2m - 15 = -9 and -5m = -15 both give m = 3.

MATH_M1.stem: A gauge fitted at an eel weir gives readings x that satisfy \(x^{4}-13x^{2}+36=0\). What is the greatest value of x that satisfies this equation?
MATH_M1.check: Treating x^2 as the unknown gives x^2 = 4 or x^2 = 9, so the four readings are -3, -2, 2 and 3.

MATH_M1.stem: A freshly cut turf weighs 5 kilograms and loses 64% of its mass while it dries on the bank. A cart carries 400 dried turves. What is the mass, in kilograms, of the cart's load?
MATH_M1.check: A dried turf keeps 36% of 5 kilograms, which is 1.8 kilograms, and 400(1.8) = 720.

MATH_M1.stem: A thatcher needs 9 bundles of straw for every 2 square metres of roof, and straw is delivered in loads of 120 bundles. A roof measures 14 metres by 6 metres. What is the least number of loads the thatcher must order to cover the roof?
MATH_M1.check: The roof is 84 square metres, which needs 84(9)/2 = 378 bundles, and 378/120 = 3.15, so 4 loads.

MATH_M1.stem:
The table gives the number of turves cut and the hours worked by each of four gangs on one peat moor.
GangTurves cutHours worked
Turf gang2,7606
Moor gang3,1507
Hill gang2,0005
Bank gang3,8408
How many more turves per hour did the fastest gang cut than the slowest gang?
MATH_M1.check: The four rates are 460, 450, 400 and 480 turves per hour, and 480 - 400 = 80.

MATH_M1.stem: A tanner recorded the masses of 12 hides and found their mean to be 25 kilograms. One hide had been entered as 18 kilograms when its true mass was 42 kilograms. Using the corrected figure, what is the mean mass, in kilograms, of the 12 hides?
MATH_M1.check: The recorded total was 12(25) = 300, the corrected total is 300 - 18 + 42 = 324, and 324/12 = 27.

MATH_M1.stem:
The table gives the result of one night's fishing, in which every trap set was recorded as either holding eels or empty.
ReachHeld eelsEmpty
Upper4515

One of the traps that held eels is picked at random. What is the probability that it was set in the lower reach?
MATH_M1.check: 45 + 75 = 120 traps held eels and 75 of them were in the lower reach, so the probability is 75/120 = 5/8.

MATH_M1.stem: On a surveyor's plan of a saltmarsh, a fence runs straight from the point (2, -3) to the point (14, 13), and one unit on the plan stands for one metre. A gate post stands at the midpoint of the fence. How many metres of fence run from the point (2, -3) to the gate post?
MATH_M1.check: The fence is the square root of 12^2 + 16^2, which is 20 metres, and the post is half way along it.

MATH_M1.stem: The concrete apron below a sluice gate is a rectangle 18 metres long and 7 metres wide. A rectangular opening 12 metres long and 2.5 metres wide is left in the middle of it for the channel, and the rest of the apron is paved. How many square metres of the apron are paved?
MATH_M1.check: The apron covers 18(7) = 126 square metres and the opening takes 12(2.5) = 30 of them, leaving 96.

MATH_M1.stem: A stop plank rests against the vertical face of a sluice weir, with its lower end on the level floor of the channel. The plank is 12 metres long and makes an angle of 60° with the face of the weir. How many metres up the face of the weir does the top of the plank reach?
MATH_M1.check: The face of the weir is the side adjacent to the 60 degree angle, so the reach is 12 cos 60, which is 6 metres.

MATH_M1.stem: A charcoal burner covers a circular floor of radius 3 metres with a mound of earth in the shape of a hemisphere. The volume of the mound is \(k\pi\) cubic metres. What is the value of k?
MATH_M1.check: A hemisphere of radius 3 has volume (2/3) times pi times 27, which is 18 pi.

MATH_M2E.stem: A fen pumping engine lifts 24 cubic metres of water each minute. At that rate, how many cubic metres does the engine lift in 7 minutes?
A hurdle maker charges 14h dollars for an order of h hurdles. One order came to $322. How many hurdles were in that order?
A withy bed carried 1,400 usable rods after 2 years and 3,000 usable rods after 6 years, and the stock grew by the same number of rods each year. By how many rods did the stock grow each year?
A reed cutter has already cut 130 bundles and now cuts 24 more bundles each day. Which expression gives the total number of bundles cut d days from now?
MATH_M2E.check: Add 24 bundles for each of the d days to the 130 already cut.

MATH_M2E.stem: A lime kiln must never be charged with more than 2,400 kilograms of limestone. Which inequality gives all the possible masses m, in kilograms, of a charge?
MATH_M2E.check: No more than 2,400 allows 2,400 itself and anything below it.

MATH_M2E.stem:
A miller's day tally gives the system
a+b=40
a-b=6
where a and b are the numbers of sacks of two grains ground that day. What is the value of a?
MATH_M2E.check: Adding the two equations gives 2a = 46, so a = 23.

MATH_M2E.stem: A basket maker works out the charge for an order as C=9n+24, where C is the charge in dollars and n is the number of baskets in the order. What does 24 represent in this model?
MATH_M2E.check: 24 does not change with n, so it is charged once for the order however many baskets it holds.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The charge, in dollars, made for each basket in the order.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A fixed charge, in dollars, made once on every order whatever its size.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The number of baskets that can be had for $9.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The greatest charge, in dollars, that can be made for one order.

MATH_M2E.stem: A basket maker uses \(4x+15\) rods for the base of a basket and \(6x-7\) rods for its sides. Which expression gives the total number of rods used for the basket?
A reed cutter models the number of bundles cut on day n as \(P(n)=n^{2}+4n\). How many bundles does the model give for day 6?
A hurdle maker's cutting rule leads to the equation \(x^{2}+5x-24=0\), which has two solutions. What is the greater of the two solutions?
MATH_M2E.check: The equation factors as (x+8)(x-3) = 0, so the solutions are -8 and 3.

MATH_M2E.stem: A lime kiln's draught is rated by \(R(t)=\frac{48}{t}+5\), where t is the number of hours since the kiln was lit. What is the rating 6 hours after lighting?
A millwright's gearing calculation uses the product \((3x^{4})(5x^{3})\). Which expression is equivalent to that product?
MATH_M2E.check: Multiply 3 by 5 and add the exponents 4 and 3.

MATH_M2E.stem: The mass of water left in a stack of drying reed is modelled by \(M(h)=640\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{h}\) kilograms, where h is the number of days of drying. What mass does the model give after 3 days?
MATH_M2E.check: 640 halved three times is 320, then 160, then 80.

MATH_M2E.stem: An osier bed yielded 450 rods, and 18% of them were rejected as too brittle. How many rods were rejected?
A watermill grinds 3 sacks of flour from every 8 bushels of wheat. At that rate, how many sacks of flour does it grind from 96 bushels of wheat?
MATH_M2E.check: 96/8 = 12 lots of 3 sacks, which is 36 sacks.

MATH_M2E.stem:
A workshop sorts the hurdles it makes into four grades, as the table records.

How many hurdles did the workshop sort altogether?
On seven days a fen pumping station logged 14, 9, 12, 20, 11, 9 and 17 hours of pumping. What is the median of the seven figures?
MATH_M2E.check: In order the figures are 9, 9, 11, 12, 14, 17, 20, and the fourth of seven is 12.

MATH_M2E.stem: Of 40 hurdles offered for inspection, 24 passed. What fraction of the hurdles failed?
Three braces meet at one point in the middle of a hurdle, and the three angles they make around that point measure 145°, 132° and x°. What is the value of x?
MATH_M2E.check: Angles round a point total 360 degrees, and 360 - 145 - 132 = 83.

MATH_M2E.stem: A rectangular reed store covers 84 square metres of ground and is 12 metres long. How wide, in metres, is the store?
A hurdle maker's yard gate is a semicircle whose straight edge is 8 metres long. The area of the gate is \(k\pi\) square metres. What is the value of k?
MATH_M2E.check: The straight edge is the diameter, so the radius is 4, a whole circle of radius 4 has area 16 pi, and half of that is 8 pi.

MATH_M2E.stem: In a right triangle set out to square a lime kiln's flue, the side opposite angle A is 7 metres long and the hypotenuse is 25 metres long. What is the value of \(\sin A\)?
MATH_M2E.check: The sine of an angle is the opposite side over the hypotenuse, which is 7/25.

MATH_M2H.stem:
A fen drainage board's costing sheet gives the system
px+4y=26
3x-qy=1
where p and q are constants. The solution of this system is x=2 and y=5. What is the value of p+q?
MATH_M2H.check: 2p + 20 = 26 gives p = 3, and 6 - 5q = 1 gives q = 1, so p + q = 4.

MATH_M2H.stem: A wind engine's daily output is a linear function g of the number of hours x that the sails turn. It is known that g(2)=7 and g(10)=31. For what value of x does this function give g(x)=100?
MATH_M2H.check: The rate is (31-7)/(10-2) = 3 and g(x) = 3x + 1, so 3x + 1 = 100 gives x = 33.

MATH_M2H.stem: A lime kiln's charge x, in tonnes, must satisfy \(3\le\frac{2x-5}{4}\le 7\). What is the greatest possible value of x?
MATH_M2H.check: Multiplying through by 4 gives 12 <= 2x-5 <= 28, so 8.5 <= x <= 16.5.

MATH_M2H.stem: At a watermill, grinding 4 sacks of wheat together with 3 sacks of barley takes 62 minutes, and grinding 6 sacks of wheat together with 5 sacks of barley takes 98 minutes. At the same rates, how many minutes does grinding 5 sacks of wheat together with 4 sacks of barley take?
MATH_M2H.check: The system gives 8 minutes a sack for wheat and 10 for barley, so 5(8) + 4(10) = 80.

MATH_M2H.stem: The number of usable rods standing in a withy bed t years after planting is modelled by \(S(t)=p-qt\), where p and q are positive constants. In terms of p and q, after how many years does the model give half as many usable rods as at planting?
MATH_M2H.check: At planting the stock is p, so p - qt = p/2 gives qt = p/2 and t = p/(2q).

MATH_M2H.stem: A basket maker has 26 hours of working time and must finish exactly 40 baskets in it. A round basket takes 20 minutes to weave and a square basket takes 45 minutes. What is the greatest number of square baskets the maker can finish within the working time?
MATH_M2H.check: 26 hours is 1,560 minutes, and 20(40-s) + 45s <= 1,560 gives 25s <= 760, so s <= 30.4 and at most 30 square baskets.

MATH_M2H.stem: Setting the gearing of a windmill leads to the equation \(\frac{2x+7}{3}-\frac{x-4}{2}=5\). What is the value of x?
MATH_M2H.check: Multiplying through by 6 gives 2(2x+7) - 3(x-4) = 30, which is x + 26 = 30.

MATH_M2H.stem: A millwright's two adjustments to a pair of stones are modelled by \(f(x)=4x+1\) and \(g(x)=x^{2}-3x\). Which expression is equivalent to \(g(f(x))-f(g(x))\)?
MATH_M2H.check: g(f(x)) is 16x^2 - 4x - 2 and f(g(x)) is 4x^2 - 12x + 1, and subtracting the second from the first leaves 12x^2 + 8x - 3.

MATH_M2H.stem: An osier grader's ratio is \(\frac{6x+19}{x+3}\), where \(x>0\). This ratio can be written as \(6+\frac{k}{x+3}\), where k is a constant. What is the value of k?
MATH_M2H.check: 6(x+3) is 6x+18, so the ratio is 6 plus a remainder of 1 over x+3.

MATH_M2H.stem: A lime burner's charging rule reduces to the equation \(9^{x+1}=27^{x-1}\). What is the value of x?
MATH_M2H.check: Writing both sides as powers of 3 gives 2x+2 = 3x-3, so x = 5.

MATH_M2H.stem: A lime kiln's fuel use is modelled by \(f(x)=x^{2}+px+q\), where p and q are constants and x is the number of hours since lighting. The model takes its least value when x=5, and it gives f(1)=9. What is the value of q?
MATH_M2H.check: The least value sits at x = -p/2, so p = -10, and 1 - 10 + q = 9 gives q = 18.

MATH_M2H.stem: A hurdle maker's scaling rule uses the expression \(2x^{3}+3x^{2}-8x-12\). Which expression is equivalent to it?
MATH_M2H.check: Grouping gives x^2(2x+3) - 4(2x+3), which is (x^2-4)(2x+3), and x^2-4 factors further.

MATH_M2H.stem: A tolerance condition on a mill's gearing gives the equation \(|2x-7|=x+1\). What is the sum of all the solutions of this equation?
MATH_M2H.check: 2x-7 = x+1 gives 8 and 7-2x = x+1 gives 2; both make x+1 positive, so the sum is 10.

MATH_M2H.stem: A gang of 6 reed cutters clears a bed in 15 days, every cutter working at the same steady rate. To clear a bed of the same size in 9 days, how many cutters must be added to the gang?
MATH_M2H.check: The work is 6(15) = 90 cutter-days, so 9 days needs 90/9 = 10 cutters, which is 4 more than the 6 already in the gang.

MATH_M2H.stem: A crate holds 9 white osier rods and 6 brown osier rods. Two rods are taken from the crate at random, one after the other, and the first is not put back. What is the probability that both rods taken are brown?
MATH_M2H.check: The first rod is brown with probability 6 out of 15 and the second with probability 5 out of 14, and the product of those is 1/7.

MATH_M2H.stem: A watermill keeps 1 sack in every 16 it grinds as its toll and returns the rest to the customers. In one week the mill kept 27 sacks as toll. How many sacks did the mill return to its customers that week?
MATH_M2H.check: 27 sacks of toll means 27(16) = 432 sacks ground, of which 432 - 27 = 405 went back.

MATH_M2H.stem: Limestone standing in a lime kiln's cylindrical shaft to a depth of 4 metres fills \(36\pi\) cubic metres of the shaft. The burner then tips in enough limestone to raise the level by a further 1.5 metres. How many cubic metres of limestone were tipped in?
MATH_M2H.check: 4 pi r^2 = 36 pi gives r^2 = 9, so each extra metre of depth is 9 pi and 1.5 metres is 13.5 pi.

MATH_M2H.stem: A hurdle maker's diagonal brace makes a right triangle whose two shorter sides are in the ratio 3 to 4 and whose longest side is 45 centimetres. What is the area, in square centimetres, of that triangle?
MATH_M2H.check: The sides are 27, 36 and 45, and half of 27 times 36 is 486.

MATH_M2H.stem: A millwright sets out a right triangle whose hypotenuse is 26 centimetres long and in which \(\sin A=\frac{5}{13}\), where A is one of the acute angles. What is the area, in square centimetres, of that triangle?
MATH_M2H.check: The side opposite A is 10 and the other leg is 24, so the area is half of 10 times 24, which is 120.

MATH_M2H.stem: A lime kiln's charging ramp is a bank of earth 20 metres long whose cross-section is the same all the way along: a right triangle whose two legs are in the ratio 3 to 4, the shorter of them being 1.5 metres. How many cubic metres of earth are in the ramp?
MATH_M2H.check: The legs are 1.5 and 2.0 metres, so the cross-section is 1.5 square metres and the ramp holds 1.5(20) = 30 cubic metres.
